title: Inside Elon Musk’s Midterm Spending Spree
gist: WIRED's Uncanny Valley podcast breaks down Elon Musk's America PAC midterm strategy: smaller but more targeted than 2024, spending more than $2 opposing Democrats for every $1 supporting Republicans in pivotal Senate races to avert a Democratic Congress and its investigations. It also covers effective altruism becoming a political wedge (Pentagon calls it a 'dangerous ideology') in the AI safety fight, and the backlash against the freelance designer paid ~$12,500 for Meta's Muse AI logo.

insights.claim: Musk's America PAC, which spent more than $260 million to elect Trump in 2024, is spending less in total for the 2026 midterms but concentrating on the most consequential Senate races that will decide control of Congress.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Signals tech-billionaire money is being deployed surgically at chamber control, raising the policy stakes of the Senate outcome for Musk-linked companies.
insights.quote: The PAC spent more than $260 million to make that happen.
insights.locator: He never really left, but he is back

insights.claim: For every dollar America PAC has spent supporting a Republican candidate, more than two dollars have gone to opposing a Democrat, a ratio that is even more extreme in key Senate races.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Negative-ad-heavy strategy suggests the goal is blocking a Democratic majority rather than building GOP allies.
insights.quote: For every dollar that America PAC has spent supporting a Republican candidate, more than two have gone to oppose a Democrat.
insights.locator: The PAC is primarily pumping money against Democrats

insights.claim: In the Texas Senate race, where several Musk companies are based, America PAC has spent roughly $9 million attacking Democrat James Talarico versus about $1 million promoting Republican Ken Paxton; similar patterns appear in Ohio and Iowa.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Texas is home-turf for Musk's businesses; heavy spending there shows where he sees regulatory exposure.
insights.locator: In Texas where several Musk companies are based

insights.claim: The targeted races represent Democrats' path to Senate control, which could expose Republicans and Musk to investigations and regulatory pressure, giving Musk a direct business motive for the spending.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: A Democratic Congress means subpoenas and oversight risk for Musk's companies (Tesla, SpaceX, xAI-linked entities).
insights.quote: They represent the path for Democrats to take control of the chamber this November and could open Republicans, Musk included, up to a lot of investigations and regulatory pressure.
insights.locator: And these races are not random

insights.claim: Democratic sources on both House and Senate sides are openly planning investigations and subpoenas the moment they take a chamber, and polls currently favor Democrats according to WIRED's politics director Leah Feiger.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Raises probability of congressional oversight hitting tech/AI firms aligned with the Trump administration in 2027.
insights.quote: Democrats are already telling us, all of our sourcing in Democrats, both on House and Senate side are hungrily talking about all of the investigations and subpoenas
insights.locator: Oh, as they should.

insights.claim: Co-host Zoë Schiffer is skeptical of the polling and expects Republicans to do 'just fine' in the midterms, a contrarian view to the prevailing Democratic-wave narrative.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Hosts disagree on the midterm outcome, underscoring uncertainty over congressional control.
insights.quote: I think Republicans are going to do just fine.
insights.locator: I mean, I am on the record

themes.theme: Musk's regulatory immunity via government dependence

insights.claim: Even if Democrats win and launch investigations, harsh regulation of Musk's empire is unlikely because the US government is heavily dependent on SpaceX and Starlink for space access and communications.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Government dependence on SpaceX is a structural moat that blunts political/regulatory downside for Musk assets.
insights.quote: I think part of the reason for that is SpaceX, and just how dependent the government is on Starlink, on SpaceX technology, on their ability to get stuff into space.
insights.locator: That said, I find it very hard

insights.claim: The only time Musk faced real accountability, over his 'funding secured' claim about taking Tesla private, the outcome was a $20 million fine, which is a rounding error relative to his wealth.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Historical enforcement precedent suggests regulatory penalties have little deterrent effect on Musk.
insights.quote: He was fined $20 million? How much is Elon Musk worth?
insights.locator: I mean, think about it. The one time

insights.claim: Musk publicly framed a Kamala Harris win as making the whole country look like California, and fear of investigations and regulation was a primary reason he went all in on Trump.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Musk's political spending is best modeled as regulatory hedging for his businesses.
insights.locator: That said, I think it is 100 percent true

insights.claim: A future 'Lina Khan-esque' regulator is the main fear for tech leaders, but the hosts argue such pressure would amount mostly to paperwork rather than real consequences for Musk.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Implies antitrust/regulatory tail risk for Musk companies may be overpriced.
insights.quote: obviously there's a clear fear that a Lina Khan-esque figure could come in and wreak havoc. But to your point, that havoc will be paperwork.
insights.locator: I think that's a really, really good point

insights.claim: Silicon Valley's loud pro-Trump donors fear a Democratic Congress would bring investigations, slow growth and cost the US the lead in AI, so they are going all in politically, while liberal rank-and-file employees donate more quietly.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Tech political spending is driven by AI-race and regulatory concerns; expect heavy tech PAC money this cycle.
insights.locator: Yeah. I mean, Silicon Valley is not a monolith.

insights.claim: A cohort of newly minted AI-research millionaires is actively debating whether to deploy their capital into philanthropy or politics, with no consensus yet.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: New AI wealth is an emerging pool of political and philanthropic capital that could shape AI policy.
insights.quote: there are a lot of newly minted millionaires, people who worked in AI research and now have a ton of money, and they are having active conversations on what is the best way to deploy
insights.locator: It's an interesting conversation in the Valley

themes.theme: Effective altruism as an AI-policy wedge

insights.claim: After AI researcher Jacob Coxon publicly backed the effective-altruist concern that advanced AI could destroy humanity, senior Pentagon officials labeled EA a 'dangerous ideology' and a Department of Defense account urged people to choose 'Americanism, not effective altruism.'
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: The administration is politicizing AI safety, raising headwinds for safety-focused labs in government business.
insights.quote: Senior Pentagon officials labeled effective altruism as a, quote, unquote, "dangerous ideology"
insights.locator: Last month, AI researcher Jacob Coxon

insights.claim: The Trump administration is using 'effective altruism' as a slur to frame AI-safety advocates as anti-growth, anti-AI-progress and therefore anti-American, delegitimizing safety arguments.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Political framing favors accelerationist labs over safety-branded ones in federal policy and procurement.
insights.quote: now you're seeing effective altruism becoming kind of like a slanderous term to say we can't and shouldn't take these people seriously.
insights.locator: But anyway, it's interesting because

insights.claim: The AI industry is commonly split into Sam Altman/OpenAI's growth-at-all-costs capitalist camp and Dario Amodei/Anthropic's EA-adjacent 'build it safely' camp, with more Anthropic researchers appearing to hold EA beliefs even though Amodei says he does not identify as EA.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Lab culture/ideology now carries political risk, which could affect government relationships and contracts.
insights.quote: Sam Altman kind of represents the growth at all costs, capitalist view of artificial intelligence. Dario represents more of the effective altruism, let's do it safely.
insights.locator: OK, this is a very, very loaded question.

insights.claim: A key critique of EA-aligned AI labs is that if a company believes it alone takes safety seriously and the stakes are extinction, it can justify almost anything to win the AI race.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Safety-branded labs may be as aggressive competitors as growth-first ones, undermining the 'safe lab' differentiation.
insights.quote: if you think that you are the only company that's taking AI safety seriously, then you "winning," quote, unquote, the AI race is really important.
insights.locator: Yeah. Yes. I think one reason

insights.claim: AI-safety concerns have gone fully mainstream, with AI safety researchers appearing on Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan, and EA featured on The Economist cover.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Mainstreaming of AI risk discourse increases odds of populist AI regulation from both left and right.
insights.locator: 100 percent. And if you thought

themes.theme: Meta Muse and the creative-labor squeeze

insights.claim: Meta's new AI assistant Muse has been an unexpected hit, still topping the app charts weeks after launch.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Early consumer traction for Meta's AI assistant is a positive signal for Meta's AI monetization.
insights.quote: it's been kind of an unexpected hit for the company. It is still topping the app charts.
insights.locator: Oh my gosh. Moving on

insights.claim: Designer Jessica Hische was paid about $12,500 for roughly two days of work designing the Muse logo and typeface, and says her corporate commissions had dried up over the past couple of years, consistent with AI eroding commercial art demand.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Evidence of AI compressing demand and pricing for commercial creative work.
insights.quote: she said in the past couple years, her corporate work had really dried up, and that she wasn't getting as many inquiries as she usually does.
insights.locator: And in fact, that is what Jessica Hische does.

insights.claim: Hische faced a three-day Threads pile-on from 'AI purist' critics for working with Meta, and argued that big tech will stop hiring human artists if those artists are attacked for it.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Anti-AI backlash may push firms to use generated assets instead of human designers, accelerating substitution.
insights.quote: These big tech companies are not going to hire artists if they feel like that artist is then going to go slam them on social media.
insights.locator: It's interesting. I asked her that question
